title: How To Inspire Classroom Management Excellence ellence/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that classroom management excellence can be built by focusing intensely on perfecting a single routine, and he specifically recommends walking in line because it happens daily, requires teamwork, occurs in public view, and serves as a reliable barometer of overall management quality. He offers a nine-step method to build that excellence: setting exacting expectations, giving an energizing pep talk, pushing the pace with urgency, offering a friendly competitive challenge, trusting students by supervising from a distance, allowing occasional relaxed breaks, publicly celebrating outside compliments, holding students accountable by starting over when standards aren't met, and genuinely praising real excellence without restraint. His central claim is that mastering one routine to a high standard transfers a broader mindset of excellence into behavior, concentration, and teamwork throughout the school day.
points: Mastering a single routine to a high standard, rather than spreading effort thin, transfers a broader excellence mindset to overall behavior.
Walking in line is recommended as the focus routine because it's daily, public, team-based, and a reliable indicator of management quality.
An energizing pep talk and a fast pace build urgency and counter boredom during routine practice.
Supervising from a distance rather than hovering communicates trust and improves performance.
Publicly acknowledged outside compliments and genuine, unrestrained praise reinforce and sustain the pursuit of excellence.
quotes: There is no reason to talk your class through something—anything—they can do perfectly well by themselves. Your students don’t need spoon-feeding. They need inspiration.
The trick to getting students to perform at a high level is to focus your class on doing one thing exceptionally well.
Performing one particular routine perfectly—with precision and focus—will transfer excellence to everything you do—behavior included.
The key is to make the act of walking in line meaningful and to tap into its inherent challenge.
Once your students get a taste of excellence, they’ll be hungry for more. But in the beginning, you need to convince them that pursuing excellence is a worthy endeavor.
Your students will do better when supervised from a distance. When you hover and micromanage you communicate your lack of faith in them.
Focusing on one thing to do extraordinary well, like walking in line, will inspire your students to pursue excellence in everything they do.
